sections.html:
Florida had 10,789,047 housing units on July 1, 2025, and an estimated 23,462,518 residents. The median owner-reported home value is $359,000 for 2020 to 2024. Population has grown 8.9 percent since April 2020, and 178,297 building permits were recorded for 2025, so new supply keeps arriving.

Owners live in 67.6 percent of homes, which means renters hold about a third. Most people stay where they are: 86.3 percent of residents aged one and older lived at the same address a year earlier. A seller therefore finds buyers among new arrivals as often as among neighbors moving up.

People 65 and older are 22.8 percent of the population, and many hold homestead benefits that change what a buyer or heir pays after a sale.

Owners with a mortgage spend a median $1,959 a month, and owners with no mortgage spend $673. Renters pay $1,669 in median gross rent. Each number is from the 2020 to 2024 estimates.

Subtract the second owner number from the first and you see what the loan itself adds. A paid-off house still costs money for taxes, insurance and upkeep. An heir holding a free-and-clear property pays less each month but faces vacancy risk, repairs and the autumn tax bill.

A median of owners' estimates differs from any recorded sale price.

Every Florida deed carries a state transfer tax called documentary stamp tax. Most counties charge 70 cents on each $100 of the price. Miami-Dade is the odd one out at 60 cents, with an added 45 cent surtax that skips a transfer of just a single-family home. The contract may say the buyer pays, but the law makes every party to the document liable.

Recording is a second cost. The clerk bills under s. 28.24(13): $5.00 for page one, $4.00 for each page after, a modernization fund charge, and a $4 per page technology fee. A short deed therefore costs little to record.

Property tax runs on its own calendar. Values are set each January 1, bills go out in November, and the early-payment discount slides from 4 percent down to 1 percent by February.

sections.h2: Homestead protection and the buyer gap
sections.html:
Save Our Homes holds a homestead's assessed value growth to the smaller of 3 percent or CPI, and a sale resets the parcel to just value the next January 1. Property without homestead is limited to 10 percent per year. That is why two neighboring houses can carry very different tax bills.

  • Read the appraiser's record for assessed and just value.
  • Ask the tax collector about any deferral or installment plan.
  • Check that an owner who moved out has not left a stale exemption behind.

A statewide median hides all of this, so local records beat averages when you are pricing.

sections.h2: County offices a seller deals with
sections.html:
Florida is split into 67 counties, and voters in each pick a sheriff, tax collector, property appraiser, supervisor of elections and clerk of the circuit court for four year terms. Only three of the five matter when you sell a house.

  • Property appraiser: sets just value every January, sends the notice in August, decides who gets an exemption.
  • Tax collector: mails the bills, accepts payment, handles deferral and installment requests, sells certificates when a bill goes unpaid.
  • Clerk of the circuit court: records your deed, collects the stamp tax, and holds foreclosure and tax deed auctions.

Calling the right office first saves days at closing.

A bill left unpaid becomes delinquent on April 1. By June 1 the tax collector auctions a tax certificate for it. Investors bid the interest rate down in quarter percent steps, and a certificate nobody wants goes to the county at the maximum rate (s. 197.432).

Nothing can be demanded from you by the certificate holder until two years after April 1 of the year the certificate was issued, and that is also when a tax deed application can start. Planning a fast sale? Pay off any delinquency before you list. Lenders insist on it, and a cash buyer's title company will insist as well.

sections.h2: Use local numbers, not the state median
sections.html:
A single statewide median mixes beach condos, inland ranch homes and rural parcels, so it cannot price your house. Start with your county, then your neighborhood, then the house itself.

County offices hold the facts that set closing costs. The appraiser publishes values, the clerk records deeds and collects stamp tax, and the tax collector sends bills. Sale price, days on market and sales volume are not in any of those statewide averages. A local agent or the clerk's recorded sales can fill that gap.

Write your questions down before you call, because each office answers only its own slice.

  • Appraiser: what are the current assessed and just values, and is every exemption still active?
  • Tax collector: are any taxes, deferrals or installment plans open against the parcel?
  • Clerk: how will the deed be recorded, and what stamp tax and recording charges will apply?

Answers vary by county, and a house in a high-growth county may be assessed very differently from a similar one inland. Treat the statewide figures above as background, then swap in county and city numbers when you set a price or plan repairs.

Closing agents can estimate settlement figures once they see the contract. Ask for a draft statement early rather than the week of closing.

Most Florida sales move in the same order. First comes a signed contract. Next the title company searches public records for liens, unpaid taxes and anyone else who has to sign. At closing the deed is signed, and the clerk records it afterward. The stamp tax is paid on that deed, and the November property tax bill is divided between buyer and seller as the contract directs.

Before listing, pull together your latest tax bill, your exemption record and any deferral or installment papers. A surprise in any of those can delay a closing by days. When the buyer pays cash there is no lender appraisal or underwriting, which leaves the title search and the payoff of any tax owed as the main timing items.

Ask the closing agent for a draft settlement statement as soon as the contract is signed, and compare each line against the office that sets it: the clerk for recording, the tax collector for property tax, the state for stamp tax.

faqs.q: What is the median home value in Florida?
faqs.a: $359,000 for 2020 to 2024. That figure is based on what owners estimate their homes are worth, so it is not a recorded sale price.

faqs.q: What share of Florida homes are owner-occupied?
faqs.a: 67.6 percent for 2020 to 2024. The state has 8,752,810 households averaging 2.51 people.

faqs.q: What does a Florida renter pay?
faqs.a: A median gross rent of $1,669 for 2020 to 2024. Owner costs are $1,959 a month with a mortgage and $673 without.

faqs.q: How many homes does Florida have?
faqs.a: 10,789,047 housing units on July 1, 2025, for a population estimated at 23,462,518.

faqs.q: Do Florida sellers face a deed tax?
faqs.a: Yes, documentary stamp tax at 70 cents per $100 of consideration in most counties. Miami-Dade charges 60 cents plus a 45 cent surtax that a single-family dwelling transfer avoids. All parties to the document are liable.
